claim: Human visual recognition activates a dense network of overlapping feedforward and recurrent neuronal processes.
source: Human visual recognition activates a dense network of overlapping feedforward and recurrent neuronal processes, making it hard to disentangle processing in the feedforward from the feedback direction.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general characterization of visual processing.

claim: Ultra-rapid serial visual presentation suppresses sustained activity that blurs the boundaries of processing steps.
source: Here, we used ultra-rapid serial visual presentation to suppress sustained activity that blurs the boundaries of processing steps, enabling us to resolve two distinct stages of processing with MEG multivariate pattern classification.
evidence: This is the main methodological premise stated in the abstract and supported by experimental results shown in Figure 4.

claim: The first processing stage was the rapid activation cascade of the bottom-up sweep, which terminated early as visual stimuli were presented at progressively faster rates.
source: The first processing stage was the rapid activation cascade of the bottom-up sweep, which terminated early as visual stimuli were presented at progressively faster rates.
evidence: This finding is supported by the peak latency data shown in Figure 2b,e and Table 1.

claim: The second stage was the emergence of categorical information with peak latency that shifted later in time with progressively faster stimulus presentations, indexing time-consuming recurrent processing.
source: The second stage was the emergence of categorical information with peak latency that shifted later in time with progressively faster stimulus presentations, indexing time-consuming recurrent processing.
evidence: This is supported by the categorical division time series shown in Figure 3a,b and Table 1.

claim: Recurrent signals were localized in early visual cortex using MEG-fMRI fusion with representational similarity.
source: Using MEG-fMRI fusion with representational similarity, we localized recurrent signals in early visual cortex.
evidence: This is supported by the MEG-fMRI fusion results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Visual information is transformed not only feedforward through ascending connections, but also from higher to lower hierarchy areas through descending feedback connections and within the same areas through lateral connections.
source: Visual information is transformed not only feedforward, as it propagates through ascending connections, but also from higher to lower hierarchy areas through descending feedback connections and within the same areas through lateral connections (Ahissar et al., 2009; Bullier, 2001; Enns and Di Lollo V, 2000; Lamme and Roelfsema, 2000; Lamme et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The concurrent activation of a dense network of anatomical connections poses a critical obstacle to the reliable measurement of recurrent signals and their segregation from feedforward activity.
source: This concurrent activation of a dense network of anatomical connections poses a critical obstacle to the reliable measurement of recurrent signals and their segregation from feedforward activity.
evidence: This is stated as a motivation for the study based on understanding of neural processing.

claim: Recent behavioral evidence exemplified the remarkable robustness of the human visual system to capture conceptual information in stimuli presented at rates of 17 or 34 ms per picture.
source: Recent behavioral evidence exemplified the remarkable robustness of the human visual system to capture conceptual information in stimuli presented at similar rates (Broers et al., 2018; Evans et al., 2011; Potter et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: Seventeen healthy subjects participated in the RSVP experiment.
source: Seventeen healthy subjects (12 female; 16 right-handed and one left-handed; age mean ± s.d. 27.2 ± 5.7 years) with normal or corrected to normal vision participated in the RSVP experiment.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental sample size.

claim: Participants viewed RSVP sequences of 11 images presented at a rate of 17 ms per picture or 34 ms per picture in separate trials.
source: Participants viewed RSVP sequences of 11 images presented at a rate of 17 ms per picture or 34 ms per picture in separate trials.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Participants performed a two-alternative forced choice task reporting whether a face was present in the sequence or not.
source: Participants performed a two-alternative forced choice task reporting whether a face was present in the sequence or not.
evidence: This describes the behavioral task used in the experiment.

claim: Participants performed the face detection task consistently above chance in the 17 ms per picture RSVP condition with d' = 1.95 ± 0.11.
source: Even though the image presentation was extremely rapid, participants performed the face detection task consistently above chance in the 17 ms per picture RSVP condition (sensitivity index d' ± SEM = 1.95 ± 0.11)
evidence: This is a direct report of behavioral performance data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Participants performed the face detection task with high accuracy in the 34 ms per picture RSVP condition with d' = 3.58 ± 0.16.
source: and with high accuracy in the 34 ms per picture RSVP condition (d' ± SEM = 3.58 ± 0.16) (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a direct report of behavioral performance data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Neural responses were resolved at the level of individual images in all 3 viewing conditions.
source: First, we found that neural responses were resolved at the level of individual images in all 3 viewing conditions.
evidence: This is supported by the decoding time series shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Decoding accuracies decreased with faster stimulus presentation rates.
source: Second, decoding accuracies decreased with faster stimulus presentation rates, reflecting the challenging nature of the RSVP task with stimuli presented for very short times.
evidence: This is evident from the decoding time series in Figure 2b showing lower accuracies for faster presentation rates.

claim: Peak latencies shifted earlier with faster stimulus presentation rates.
source: Third, peak latencies shifted earlier with faster stimulus presentation rates (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is supported by the peak latency analysis shown in Figure 2e and Table 1.

claim: The 500 ms per picture condition reached a peak at 121 ms (95% confidence interval: 102-126 ms).
source: That is, the 500 ms per picture condition reached a peak at 121 ms (95% confidence interval: 102-126 ms)
evidence: This is a direct report of peak latency data shown in Figure 2e and Table 1.

claim: The 34 ms per picture RSVP condition reached a peak at 100 ms (94-107 ms).
source: preceded by the 34 ms per picture RSVP condition at 100 ms (94-107 ms)
evidence: This is a direct report of peak latency data shown in Figure 2e and Table 1.

claim: The 17 ms per picture RSVP condition reached a peak at 96 ms (93-99 ms).
source: and finally the 17 ms per picture RSVP condition at 96 ms (93-99 ms)
evidence: This is a direct report of peak latency data shown in Figure 2e and Table 1.

claim: Onset latencies shifted later with faster stimulus presentation rates.
source: Fourth, onset latencies shifted later with faster stimulus presentation rates (Figure 2h).
evidence: This is supported by the onset latency analysis shown in Figure 2h and Table 1.

claim: The 500 ms per picture condition had onset at 28 ms (9-53 ms).
source: That is, the 500 ms per picture condition had onset at 28 ms (9-53 ms)
evidence: This is a direct report of onset latency data shown in Figure 2h and Table 1.

claim: The 34 ms per picture RSVP condition had onset at 64 ms (58-69 ms).
source: followed by the 34 ms per picture RSVP condition at 64 ms (58-69 ms)
evidence: This is a direct report of onset latency data shown in Figure 2h and Table 1.

claim: The 17 ms per picture RSVP condition had onset at 70 ms (63-76 ms).
source: and finally the 17 ms per picture RSVP condition at 70 ms (63-76 ms)
evidence: This is a direct report of onset latency data shown in Figure 2h and Table 1.

claim: The highest levels of the visual processing hierarchy in humans are reached within the first 100 ms.
source: Even though the highest levels of the visual processing hierarchy in humans are reached with the first 100 ms, there is little time for feedback connections from these areas to exert an effect (Lamme and Roelfsema, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Neural activity during the first 100 ms has been linked to the engagement of feedforward and local recurrent connections, rather than long-range feedback connections.
source: Thus, neural activity during the first 100 ms has been linked to the engagement of feedforward and local recurrent connections, rather than long-range feedback connections.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on cited literature and the timing of neural responses.

claim: The early peaks at 100 and 96 ms for the 34 and 17 ms per picture RSVP conditions explicitly delineate the first sweep of visual activity, differentiating it from later neural activity that includes feedback influences from the top of the visual hierarchy.
source: In line with these arguments, the early peaks at 100 and 96 ms for the 34 and 17 ms per picture RSVP conditions, respectively, explicitly delineate the first sweep of visual activity, differentiating it from later neural activity that includes feedback influences from the top of the visual hierarchy.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the peak latency data in the context of visual processing theory.

claim: Different stimulus durations have different onset latencies, suggesting that interactions with recurrent activity are already incorporated when the first decoding onsets emerge.
source: The fact that different stimulus durations have different onsets suggests that interactions with recurrent activity are already incorporated when the first decoding onsets emerge, arguing against the view that the early part of the decoding time course can be uniquely tied to feedforward alone (Fahrenfort et al., 2012; Lamme and Roelfsema, 2000; Ringach et al., 1997).
evidence: This is an inference from the onset latency data combined with cited literature.

claim: Individual images were discriminated by neural responses within faces and objects categories.
source: We confirmed the generalization and reliability of our findings, as our results were similar to the grand total decoding time series: individual images were discriminated by neural responses
evidence: This is supported by the within-category decoding time series shown in Figure 2c,d.

claim: The categorical division time series resolved face versus object information in all three conditions.
source: We found that the categorical division time series resolved face versus object information in all three conditions (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by the categorical division time series shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Categorical neural representations were stronger in the 500 and 34 ms per picture conditions than the 17 ms per picture condition.
source: Consistent with the grand total decoding results, categorical neural representations were stronger in the 500 and 34 ms per picture conditions than the 17 ms per picture condition.
evidence: This is evident from the categorical division time series in Figure 3a showing higher values for slower presentation rates.

claim: The time series for the 500 ms per picture condition peaked at 136 ms (130-139 ms).
source: That is, the time series for the 500 ms per picture condition peaked at 136 ms (130-139 ms)
evidence: This is a direct report of peak latency data for categorical division shown in Figure 3b and Table 1.

claim: The 34 ms per picture RSVP peaked at 169 ms (165-177 ms).
source: followed by the 34 ms per picture RSVP at 169 ms (165-177 ms)
evidence: This is a direct report of peak latency data for categorical division shown in Figure 3b and Table 1.

claim: The 17 ms per picture RSVP peaked at 197 ms (184-218 ms).
source: and the 17 ms per picture RSVP at 197 ms (184-218 ms)
evidence: This is a direct report of peak latency data for categorical division shown in Figure 3b and Table 1.

claim: The peak latency relationship for categorical information is reverse from the peak latency of the first sweep of visual activity.
source: This relationship is reverse from the peak latency of the first sweep of visual activity reported in the previous section, further stressing the existence of variable dynamics in the ventral pathway.
evidence: This is a comparison of the peak latency patterns between Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Categorical information did not arise directly in a purely feedforward mode of processing.
source: This suggests that categorical information did not arise directly in a purely feedforward mode of processing, as this would predict comparable temporal dynamics in all conditions.
evidence: This is an inference from the variable peak latencies of categorical information across conditions.

claim: Recurrent interactions within the ventral stream facilitate the emergence of categorical information by enhancing stimulus information in challenging visual tasks.
source: Instead, it is consistent with the idea that recurrent interactions within the ventral stream facilitate the emergence of categorical information by enhancing stimulus information in challenging visual tasks (Brincat and Connor, 2006; Hochstein and Ahissar, 2002; Rajaei et al., 2018; Tang and Kreiman, 2017; Tapia and Beck, 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Neural activity became increasingly transient at rapid presentation rates.
source: Our temporal generalization analysis confirmed that neural activity became increasingly transient at rapid presentation rates (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by the temporal generalization matrices shown in Figure 4.

claim: The 500 ms per picture condition had maps with broad off-diagonal significant elements characteristic of sustained representations.
source: While the 500 ms per picture condition had maps with broad off-diagonal significant elements characteristic of sustained representations
evidence: This is evident from the temporal generalization matrix in Figure 4a.

claim: The RSVP conditions had narrow diagonal maps indicating transient neural patterns.
source: the RSVP conditions had narrow diagonal maps indicating transient neural patterns, with the 17 ms per picture RSVP narrower than the 34 ms per picture RSVP.
evidence: This is evident from the temporal generalization matrices in Figure 4b,c.

claim: The time series peaked earlier for EVC than IT in all conditions.
source: In all conditions, consistent with the view of visual processing as a spatiotemporal cascade (Cichy et al., 2014), the time series peaked earlier for EVC than IT (Figure 5c–h).
evidence: This is supported by the MEG-fMRI representational similarity time series shown in Figure 5c-e.

claim: The peak-to-peak latency between EVC and IT was 27 ms for the 500 ms per picture condition.
source: The peak-to-peak latency between EVC and IT increased as viewing conditions became increasingly challenging with faster presentation rates: Δ=27 ms for the 500 ms per picture condition
evidence: This is calculated from the peak latencies shown in Figure 5f and Table 2.

claim: The peak-to-peak latency between EVC and IT was 79 ms for the 34 ms per picture RSVP.
source: Δ=79 ms for the 34 ms per picture RSVP
evidence: This is calculated from the peak latencies shown in Figure 5g and Table 2.

claim: The peak-to-peak latency between EVC and IT was 115 ms for the 17 ms per picture RSVP.
source: and Δ=115 ms for the 17 ms per picture RSVP
evidence: This is calculated from the peak latencies shown in Figure 5h and Table 2.

claim: The EVC peak had progressively shorter latencies (104 vs. 87 vs. 80 ms for the 3 conditions).
source: First, the EVC peak had progressively shorter latencies (104 vs. 87 vs. 80 ms for the 3 conditions)
evidence: This is a summary of the EVC peak latencies shown in Figure 5c-e and Table 2.

claim: The IT peak had progressively longer latencies (131 vs. 166 vs. 195 ms for the three conditions).
source: and second the IT peak had progressively longer latencies (131 vs. 166 vs. 195 ms for the three conditions).
evidence: This is a summary of the IT peak latencies shown in Figure 5c-e and Table 2.

claim: EVC had a single peak at 104 ms and persistent representations over hundreds of milliseconds for the 500 ms per picture condition.
source: Importantly, while EVC had a single peak at 104 ms and persistent representations over hundreds of milliseconds for the 500 ms per picture condition
evidence: This is evident from the EVC time series in Figure 5c.

claim: EVC dynamics were transient and bimodal for the RSVP conditions.
source: its dynamics were transient and bimodal for the RSVP conditions.
evidence: This is evident from the EVC time series in Figure 5d,e showing two peaks.

claim: For the 34 ms per picture RSVP condition, an early peak at 87 ms was immediately followed by weak MEG-fMRI representational similarities, and then a second peak at 169 ms.
source: For the 34 ms per picture RSVP condition, an early peak at 87 ms was immediately followed by weak MEG-fMRI representational similarities, and then a second peak at 169 ms.
evidence: This is a description of the EVC time series shown in Figure 5d and Table 2.

claim: For the 17 ms per picture RSVP condition, an early peak at 80 ms was followed by a second peak at 202 ms.
source: For the 17 ms per picture RSVP condition, we observed similar dynamics with an early peak at 80 ms and a second peak at 202 ms
evidence: This is a description of the EVC time series shown in Figure 5e and Table 2.

claim: The second peak in EVC occurred at similar times as the peak in IT for the 34 ms per picture RSVP condition (Δ=3 ms, p=0.06).
source: The second peak in EVC occurred at similar times as the peak in IT (Δ=3 ms for the 34 ms per picture RSVP condition, p=0.06
evidence: This is a comparison of peak latencies between EVC and IT shown in Figure 5d,g and Table 2.

claim: The second peak in EVC is consistent with feedback activity in EVC at the same time as IT solves visual object recognition.
source: This is consistent with feedback activity in EVC at the same time as IT solves visual object recognition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the synchronous peaks in EVC and IT.

claim: Resolving feedback activity in EVC was possible with MEG-fMRI fusion because MEG activation patterns disentangled slow fMRI hemodynamic responses in EVC that correspond to the combined contributions of feedforward and feedback visual activity.
source: We note here that resolving feedback activity in EVC was possible with MEG-fMRI fusion because MEG activation patterns disentangled slow fMRI hemodynamic responses in EVC that correspond to the combined contributions of feedforward and feedback visual activity.
evidence: This is an explanation of the methodological advantage of MEG-fMRI fusion.

claim: The ultra-RSVP task enabled demarcation of two different processing stages in the ventral stream.
source: Taken together, the ultra-RSVP task enabled us to demarcate two different processing stages in the ventral stream, segregate the initial bottom-up sweep from late categorical signals, characterize the delay of the emergence of categorical information as an index of increased recurrent processing demands, and localize feedback activity in EVC.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Most popular computer vision models have adopted a feedforward architecture to sequentially transform visual signals into complex representations.
source: Most popular computer vision models, such as deep neural networks (LeCun et al., 2015) and HMAX (Riesenhuber and Poggio, 1999), have adopted a feedforward architecture to sequentially transform visual signals into complex representations, akin to the human ventral stream.
evidence: This is a statement about computational models supported by citations.

claim: Deep neural networks and HMAX achieve accuracy on par with human performance in many tasks.
source: Recent work has shown that these models not only achieve accuracy in par with human performance in many tasks (He et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Deep neural networks and HMAX share a hierarchical correspondence with neural object representations.
source: but also share a hierarchical correspondence with neural object representations (Cichy et al., 2016b; Martin Cichy et al., 2017; Yamins et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Models with purely feedforward architecture often mislabel objects in challenging conditions.
source: Even though models with purely feedforward architecture can easily recognize whole objects (Serre et al., 2007), they often mislabel objects in challenging conditions, such as incongruent object-background pairings, or ambiguous and partially occluded inputs (Johnson and Olshausen, 2005; O'Reilly et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Models that incorporate recurrent connections are robust to partially occluded objects.
source: Instead, models that incorporate recurrent connections are robust to partially occluded objects (O'Reilly et al., 2013; Rajaei et al., 2018), suggesting the importance of recurrent processing for object recognition.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The RSVP paradigm has been implemented with stimulus rates about 100 ms per item or slower since its conception.
source: Since its conception (Potter and Levy, 1969), the RSVP paradigm has been implemented with stimulus rates about 100 ms per item or slower.
evidence: This is a historical statement about the RSVP paradigm supported by citation.

claim: Behavioral investigations have been exploring presentation rates of 13 to 20 ms per picture in ultra-RSVP tasks.
source: Recently however, behavioral investigations have been exploring even faster presentation rates in ultra-RSVP tasks (Broers et al., 2018; Evans et al., 2011; Potter et al., 2014). These experiments found that observers can detect target images at rates 13 to 20 ms per picture.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: High behavioral performance in the ultra-RSVP task has been used as an argument to support the view that a purely feedforward mode of processing is sufficient to extract meaning from complex natural scenes.
source: One view posits that a purely feedforward mode of processing is sufficient to extract meaning from complex natural scenes (DiCarlo et al., 2012). High behavioral performance in the ultra-RSVP task has been used as an argument to support this view.
evidence: This is a statement about an interpretation of ultra-RSVP results supported by citation.

claim: Rapid presentations of stimuli have been presumed to block recurrent activity, since low level visual representations are immediately overwritten by subsequent images and time is too short to allow multiple synaptic transmissions.
source: Specifically, such rapid presentations of stimuli have been presumed to block recurrent activity, since low level visual representations are immediately overwritten by subsequent images and time is too short to allow multiple synaptic transmissions (Tovée, 1994).
evidence: This is a statement about a theoretical interpretation supported by citation.

claim: The ability to detect and categorize images at ultra-RSVP speeds depends on the efficacy of the images to mask one another.
source: However, this interpretation has been challenged both here, with the reengagement of EVC late in the processing stream, and by the finding that the ability to detect and categorize images at such speeds depends on the efficacy of the images to mask one another (Maguire and Howe, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature and the current findings.

claim: The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
source: The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and followed the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: The stimulus set comprised 24 target images (12 faces and 12 objects) and 45 mask images of various object categories.
source: The stimulus set comprised 24 target images (12 faces and 12 objects) and 45 mask images of various object categories (Figure 1a).
evidence: This describes the experimental stimulus set.

claim: MEG data was collected using a 306-channel Elekta Triux system with a 1000 Hz sampling rate.
source: We collected MEG data using a 306-channel Elekta Triux system with a 1000 Hz sampling rate.
evidence: This describes the MEG data acquisition parameters.

claim: The data was band-pass filtered with cut-off frequencies of 0.03 and 330 Hz.
source: The data was band-pass filtered with cut-off frequencies of 0.03 and 330 Hz.
evidence: This describes the MEG data preprocessing.

claim: Time-resolved multivariate pattern classification was used to track how neural representations resolved stimulus information in time.
source: To track how neural representations resolved stimulus information in time, we used time-resolved multivariate pattern classification on the MEG data (Cichy and Pantazis, 2017; Cichy et al., 2014; Isik et al., 2014; King and Dehaene, 2014).
evidence: This describes the analysis method supported by citations.

claim: Support vector machine classifiers were used to discriminate pairs of target images.
source: For each time point separately, we used the MEG data to classify pairwise (50% chance level) all 24 target images.
evidence: This describes the classification procedure.

claim: Sixteen participants viewed the same 24 target images in isolation in a separate MEG experiment at 500 ms per picture.
source: In a separate MEG experiment, a different cohort of 16 healthy participants view the same 24 target images in isolation. Images were presented in random order for 500 ms with an ISI of 1 s.
evidence: This describes a control experiment with different participants.

claim: Fifteen participants viewed the same 24 target images in an fMRI experiment.
source: The same 24 target images were also presented to a different cohort of 15 healthy participants in an fMRI experiment.
evidence: This describes the fMRI experiment with different participants.

claim: fMRI data was collected using a 3T Trio Siemens Scanner and 32-channel head coil.
source: The fMRI data was collected using a 3T Trio Siemens Scanner and 32-channel head coil.
evidence: This describes the fMRI data acquisition parameters.

claim: V1 was defined separately for each participant using an anatomical eccentricity template corresponding to a 0–6° visual angle.
source: V1 was defined separately for each participant using an anatomical eccentricity template (Benson et al., 2012), and corresponded to a 0–6° visual angle.
evidence: This describes the ROI definition procedure supported by citation.

claim: IT was defined using a mask comprising bilateral fusiform and inferior temporal cortex.
source: IT was defined using a mask comprising bilateral fusiform and inferior temporal cortex (Maldjian et al., 2003)
evidence: This describes the ROI definition procedure supported by citation.

claim: Representational similarity analysis was used to assess the spatiotemporal dynamics of EVC and IT.
source: To assess the spatiotemporal dynamics of EVC and IT, we applied a fMRI-MEG fusion approach based on representational similarity analysis (RSA) (Kriegeskorte et al., 2008; Cichy et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the analysis method supported by citations.

claim: The basic idea of RSA is that if two stimuli are similarly represented in MEG patterns, they should also be similarly represented in fMRI patterns.
source: The basic idea is that if two stimuli are similarly represented in MEG patterns, they should also be similarly represented in fMRI patterns, a correspondence that can be directly evaluated using the RDMs.
evidence: This explains the principle of representational similarity analysis.

claim: Statistical inference relied on non-parametric statistical tests that do not make assumptions on the distributions of the data.
source: Statistical inference relied on non-parametric statistical tests that do not make assumptions on the distributions of the data (Maris and Oostenveld, 2007; Pantazis et al., 2005).
evidence: This describes the statistical approach supported by citations.

claim: Permutation-based cluster-size inference was performed for the statistical assessment of classification time series, temporal generalization matrices, and MEG-fMRI representational similarities.
source: Specifically, for the statistical assessment of classification time series, temporal generalization matrices, and MEG-fMRI representational similarities we performed permutation-based cluster-size inference.
evidence: This describes the statistical testing procedure.

claim: The extent of disruption of the initial sweep is related to longer processing times at subsequent stages to solve visual recognition.
source: This reverse relation of the peak latencies between the two processing stages has two critical implications: first, the extent of disruption of the initial sweep is related to longer processing times at subsequent stages to solve visual recognition
evidence: This is an interpretation of the inverse relationship between early and late peak latencies.

claim: Variable temporal dynamics index the existence of recurrent activity in the ventral pathway that takes up additional processing time to solve visual recognition when initial signals are limited in time.
source: and second, such variable temporal dynamics index the existence of recurrent activity in the ventral pathway that takes up additional processing time to solve visual recognition when initial signals are limited in time.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the variable temporal dynamics across conditions.

claim: Recurrent connections have often been thought to subserve slower top-down attentional modulations from frontoparietal sites once recognition has been solved.
source: Recurrent connections have often been thought to subserve slower top-down attentional modulations from frontoparietal sites once recognition has been solved (Bar et al., 2006; Hopf et al., 2006; Sehatpour et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a statement about a theoretical view supported by citations.

claim: The study corroborates growing experimental evidence suggesting that recurrent signals also originate from within the ventral pathway as recognition unfolds, and can exert their influence before attentional modulations.
source: In contrast, our study corroborates growing experimental evidence suggesting that recurrent signals also originate from within the ventral pathway as recognition unfolds, and can exert their influence before attentional modulations (Boehler et al., 2008; Wyatte et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Extensive evidence suggests the existence of rapid feedback signals using highly controlled artificial stimuli.
source: Third, while extensive evidence suggests the existence of rapid feedback signals using highly controlled artificial stimuli, such as Kanizsa-type illusory figures, motion of random dots, and oriented bars (Halgren et al., 2003; Hupé et al., 1998; Lamme et al., 2002; Murray et al., 2002; Ringach et al., 1997; Wokke et al., 2012, 2013; Yoshino et al., 2006), it is not clear whether these results generalize to real-world situations.
evidence: This is a statement about prior research supported by multiple citations.

claim: The study demonstrated the existence of feedback activity in early visual cortex under more ecologically valid conditions using natural images of objects and faces.
source: Since our target stimuli were natural images of objects and faces, we demonstrated the existence of feedback activity in early visual cortex under more ecologically valid conditions.
evidence: This is a claim about the ecological validity of the findings.

claim: Temporal delays in processing stimulus information have been observed when visibility conditions were impoverished.
source: Fourth, even though temporal delays in processing stimulus information have been observed when visibility conditions were impoverished (Tang and Kreiman, 2017), here we explicitly related bottom-up and feedback dynamics to each other and offered well-defined temporal signatures for both mechanisms.
evidence: This is a statement about prior research supported by citation.

claim: The brain compensates for early disruptions of the initial sweep through longer processing times at subsequent stages.
source: Our results thus allow the identification of three fundamental processing principles of object recognition: (i) the brain compensates for early disruptions of the initial sweep through longer processing times at subsequent stages
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding of the study.

claim: Delays in solving object recognition are an index of increased recurrent processing.
source: (ii) delays in solving object recognition are an index of increased recurrent processing
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding of the study.

claim: Recurrent processing takes place in early visual cortex and coincides in time with the emergence of categorical information in inferior-temporal cortex.
source: and (iii) such recurrent processing takes place in early visual cortex and coincides in time with the emergence of categorical information in inferior-temporal cortex.
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding of the study.

claim: Neurons remain active even after their initial contribution in the feedforward sweep in typical viewing conditions, with their responses modulated with contextual information both within and outside their receptive fields.
source: In typical viewing conditions, such as the 500 ms per picture condition used here, neurons are known to remain active even after their initial contribution in the feedforward sweep, with their responses modulated with contextual information both within and outside their receptive fields (Lamme and Roelfsema, 2000).
evidence: This is a statement about neural processing supported by citation.

claim: Dynamic orientation tuning of V1 cell responses is shaped by horizontal intracortical connections.
source: Examples include the dynamic orientation tuning of V1 cell responses, which is shaped by horizontal intracortical connections (Ringach et al., 1997)
evidence: This is an example of local recurrent processing supported by citation.

claim: Segregation of texture is shaped by feedback signals from extrastriate areas.
source: and the segregation of texture, which is shaped by feedback signals from extrastriate areas (Hupé et al., 1998; Lamme et al., 1998).
evidence: This is an example of feedback processing supported by citations.

claim: Experiments using transcranial magnetic stimulation, backward masking, and reversible cooling offer evidence that rapid feedback circuits in the ventral pathway are engaged within the first 80–150 ms of vision.
source: Experiments using transcranial magnetic stimulation (Camprodon et al., 2010; Koivisto et al., 2011), backward masking (Boehler et al., 2008; Fahrenfort et al., 2007; Kovács et al., 1995; Lamme et al., 2002), and reversible cooling (Hupé et al., 1998) offer evidence that rapid feedback circuits in the ventral pathway are engaged within the first 80–150 ms of vision
evidence: This is a statement about prior research supported by multiple citations.

claim: Local feedback signals from extrastriate areas to V1 emerge within 80–110 ms.
source: with local feedback signals from extrastriate areas to V1 emerging within 80–110 ms (Wyatte et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the timing of feedback signals supported by citation.

claim: Reduced early recurrent activity in the RSVP conditions could be due to shorter stimulus presentation times resulting in limited stimulus evidence accumulation.
source: Reduced early recurrent activity in the RSVP conditions could be due to two reasons. First, shorter stimulus presentation times resulted in limited stimulus evidence accumulation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the reduced early activity in RSVP conditions.

claim: Reduced early recurrent activity in the RSVP conditions could be due to mask stimuli disrupting recurrent processing of the target.
source: And second, the mask stimuli disrupted recurrent processing of the target in the RSVP conditions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the reduced early activity in RSVP conditions.

claim: Delays in neural responses have been used as an indicator of recurrent computations in previous studies.
source: Such delays in neural responses have been used as an indicator of recurrent computations in previous studies, including object selective responses in human fusiform gyri for partially visible images (Tang and Kreiman, 2017) and the integration of object parts into a coherent representation in macaque posterior IT (Brincat and Connor, 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about prior research supported by citations.

claim: An alternative explanation of the variable peak latencies due to delayed propagation of feedforward signals is unlikely.
source: An alternative explanation of the variable peak latencies due to delayed propagation of feedforward signals is unlikely.
evidence: This is an argument against an alternative interpretation.

claim: Reengagement of EVC is consistent with theories positing that feedback signals serve to add details in an initially established scene.
source: Reengagement of EVC is consistent with theories positing that feedback signals serve to add details in an initially established scene (Hochstein and Ahissar, 2002; Peyrin et al., 2010; Tapia and Beck, 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the EVC reengagement supported by citations.

claim: When stimuli are degraded, partial, or otherwise ambiguous, recurrent processes fill-in stimulus information by propagating partial responses back to EVC and activating neurons that would normally respond to the complete stimulus.
source: According to these theories, when stimuli are degraded, partial, or otherwise ambiguous, recurrent processes fill-in stimulus information by propagating partial responses back to EVC and activating neurons that would normally respond to the complete stimulus (Muckli et al., 2015; O'Reilly et al., 2013; Tang and Kreiman, 2017; Wyatte et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about theoretical mechanisms supported by citations.

claim: Recurrent activity may have filled-in missing visual information necessary to recognize the face target images.
source: Thus, here recurrent activity may have filled-in missing visual information necessary to recognize the face target images.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional role of recurrent activity.

claim: Relatively modest shifts in the latency of categorical information encoded rapidly in the ventral stream have been linked to corresponding shifts in behavioral response delays.
source: Such information is probably behaviorally relevant, as even relatively modest shifts in the latency of categorical information encoded rapidly in the ventral stream have been linked to corresponding shifts in behavioral response delays (Cauchoix et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the behavioral relevance of neural timing supported by citation.

claim: Rapid recurrent signals originating within the ventral pathway are involuntary.
source: Rapid recurrent signals originating within the ventral pathway are involuntary (Roland et al., 2006)
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of recurrent signals supported by citation.

claim: Rapid recurrent signals are temporally dissociable from top-down attentional signals that are typically reported at later times.
source: and temporally dissociable from top-down attentional signals that are typically reported at later times (Boehler et al., 2008; Wyatte et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the timing of different types of signals supported by citations.

claim: The experimental design used a delayed response design for the RSVP conditions with response prompted 0.7–1 s after the offset of the stimulus.
source: First, our experimental design used a delayed response design for the RSVP conditions (response was prompted 0.7–1 s after the offset of the stimulus), and no response for the 500 ms per picture condition.
evidence: This describes the experimental design to minimize motor artifacts.

claim: Motor artifacts, including motor preparation signals, should have been delayed considerably for the RSVP conditions.
source: Thus any motor artifacts, including motor preparation signals, should have been delayed considerably for the RSVP conditions, and are completely absent in the 500 ms per picture condition.
evidence: This is an inference about the timing of potential motor artifacts.

claim: The analysis to localize processes with fMRI-MEG fusion supports the source of categorical information in IT.
source: Second, we believe that our analysis to localize these processes with fMRI-MEG fusion supports the source of categorical information in IT.
evidence: This is a statement about the localization of categorical information.

claim: Previous studies have shown that motor-preparation signals occur considerably later (300-400 ms after stimulus onset).
source: Third, previous studies have shown that motor-preparation signals occurs considerably later (300-400 ms after stimulus onset) (Thorpe et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a statement about the timing of motor signals supported by citation.

claim: It is unlikely the effects before 200 ms from stimulus onset reported in the data are related to motor preparation.
source: Thus it is unlikely the effects before 200 ms from stimulus onset reported in our data are related to motor preparation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of motor preparation signals.

claim: Computational models with recursive architecture should solve object categorization within the first couple hundred milliseconds, even when the feedforward and feedback pathways are compromised as in the ultra-RSVP task.
source: First, such models should solve object categorization within the first couple hundred milliseconds, even when the feedforward and feedback pathways are compromised as in the ultra-RSVP task.
evidence: This is a recommendation for computational models based on the findings.

claim: The timing of recurrent processes in computational models should not be predetermined and fixed, but vary depending on viewing conditions.
source: Second, the timing of recurrent processes should not be predetermined and fixed, but vary depending on viewing conditions, as in the case of onset and peak latency shifts in the RSVP decoding time series.
evidence: This is a recommendation for computational models based on the findings.

claim: The timing and strength of the early visual signals should inversely determine the timing of categorical representations in computational models.
source: Third, the timing and strength of the early visual signals should inversely determine the timing of categorical representations.
evidence: This is a recommendation for computational models based on the findings.

claim: Feedback processes in deep models should activate early layers of the model at the same time object representations are emerging at the last layers.
source: And fourth, feedback processes in deep models should activate early layers of the model at the same time object representations are emerging at the last layers.
evidence: This is a recommendation for computational models based on the findings.

claim: Future research is needed to understand what recurrent computations are exactly carried out by the brain to solve visual recognition under RSVP-like presentation conditions.
source: Despite these insights, future research is needed to understand what recurrent computations are exactly carried out by the brain to solve visual recognition under RSVP-like presentation conditions.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: RSVP experiments have revealed the temporal limitations of human perception, attention, and memory.
source: Inherent to the design, RSVP experiments have revealed the temporal limitations of human perception (Spence, 2002), attention (Nieuwenstein and Potter, 2006), and memory (Potter, 1993).
evidence: This is a statement about prior RSVP research supported by citations.

claim: Observers can detect target images at rates 13 to 20 ms per picture in ultra-RSVP tasks.
source: These experiments found that observers can detect target images at rates 13 to 20 ms per picture.
evidence: This is a statement about behavioral findings in ultra-RSVP tasks.

claim: The ultra-RSVP paradigm could be used to address the question whether recurrent processing is necessary for recognition of objects.
source: Due to its effectiveness in masking stimuli by combining forward and backward masking, the ultra-RSVP paradigm could be used to address the question whether recurrent processing is necessary for recognition of objects.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential use of ultra-RSVP.

claim: It remains an open question whether recurrent activity is necessary to extract conceptual meaning.
source: Thus, it still remains an open question whether recurrent activity is necessary to extract conceptual meaning (Howe, 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about an open research question supported by citation.

claim: The study paves the way for future studies to explore the link between stimulus visibility and recurrent neuronal processes.
source: Though our study did not address whether such recurrent activity can arise in more effective masking conditions that suppress visibility (Maguire and Howe, 2016), it paves the way for future studies to explore the link between stimulus visibility and recurrent neuronal processes.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Future studies could vary the effectiveness of forward and backward masking to segregate the early from late visual signals and investigate under what conditions stimulus visibility is associated with feedback activity.
source: Such studies could vary the effectiveness of forward and backward masking to segregate the early from late visual signals, as accomplished here, and investigate under what conditions (e.g. ambiguous or occluded input) stimulus visibility (King et al., 2016; Salti et al., 2015) is associated with feedback activity.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research supported by citations.

claim: Ultra-RSVP reduces visibility.
source: As ultra-RSVP reduces visibility, future studies could also investigate whether recurrent activity is an integral component of the neural correlates of consciousness
evidence: This is a statement about the effect of ultra-RSVP on visibility.

claim: Future studies could investigate whether recurrent activity is an integral component of the neural correlates of consciousness.
source: future studies could also investigate whether recurrent activity is an integral component of the neural correlates of consciousness, defined as the minimum neuronal mechanisms jointly sufficient for a conscious percept (Koch et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research supported by citation.
